question: Annex I of EU Directive 2009/54/EC1 requires ‘natural mineral water’ and ‘spring water’ to maintain their natural state and purity. Labelling a water as such implies premium quality and generally commands a higher price. However, recent scientific studies have shown many bottled waters to contain microplastics23. This casts serious doubts on the definition and marketing of products as ‘natural mineral water’ or ‘spring water’, as it contradicts the very idea that these waters are ‘pure’ or in a ‘natural state’. 1.

In light of this, does the Commission consider that using the terms ‘spring water’ and ‘natural mineral water’ could mislead consumers when micro- and nano-plastics can be traced in almost all types of drinking water, regardless of provenance?
Given the danger that micro- and nano-plastics can pose to human health, would the Commission consider phasing-out the use of plastic bottles in the EU?
And as groundwater pollution from pesticide residues, PFAS and other chemicals is becoming more common, does the Commission consider that aspirations to ‘purity’ might become impossible to achieve?

Directive 2009/54/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 June 2009 on the exploitation and marketing of natural mineral waters, OJ L 164, 26.6.2009, p. 45. https://www.cvua-mel.de/index.php/aktuell/138-untersuchung-von-mikroplastik-in-lebensmitteln-undkosmetika. Often, the occurrence of microplastics is linked to PET-bottles (re-usable and single-use ones).
However, even waters sold in glass bottles have been shown to contain microplastics, while determining the source of the contamination remains almost impossible. https://orbmedia.org/plus-plastic.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.7.2024) Directive 2009/54/EC1 provides for clear requirements for natural mineral waters and spring waters to be marketed as such and for measures to be taken in case of non-compliance with its provisions. The EU rules in place aim to pursue a high level of protection of consumers’ health and interests, to protect consumers from being misled and to ensure fair trading.

Member States are responsible for efficiently enforcing the EU rules to ensure that consumers are not misled. The use of single-use plastic bottles in the EU is covered by the Single-Use Plastics Directive2 including measures on product design, extended producer responsibility, separate collection and awareness raising.

The evaluation of the Directive by 2027 will analyse existing measures and might propose additional measures on single-use plastic bottles, if appropriate. The Commission is already strengthening the EU legal framework to tackle water pollution.

In October 2022 the legislative proposal on ‘Integrated Water Management’3 was introduced aiming to review the lists of pollutants affecting surface water and groundwater and corresponding their regulatory standards. The proposal includes new groups of substances to be considered in groundwater4 and introduces provisions for the monitoring of microplastics.

The Commission has also revised the Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive (UWWTD)5 and the Industrial Emissions Directive (IED)6 to further reduce the amount of pollution discharged in the environment and in water bodies. The recast of the UWWTD text has recently been agreed by the co-legislators, and the final vote will take place in October 2024.
The IED has recently been adopted by the co-legislators and will soon enter into force.
1 Directive 2009/54/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 18 June 2009 on the exploitation and

marketing of natural mineral waters (Recast), OJ L 164, 26.6.2009, p. 45–58. 2 Directive (EU) 2019/904 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 5 June 2019 on the reduction of the impact of certain plastic products on the environment, OJ L 155, 12.6.2019, p. 1–19.

3 Proposal for a Directive amending the Water Framework Directive, the Groundwater Directive and the Environmental Quality Standards Directive https://environment.ec.europa.eu/publications/proposal-amendingwater-directives_en; currently in co-decision. 4 Some examples include Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), pharmaceuticals and non-relevant metabolites of pesticides.

5 Urban wastewater – Ensuring that urban wastewater is properly dealt with to protect the environment and human health - https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/water/urban-wastewater_en 6 Industrial Emissions Directive – Preventing and controlling industrial emissions https://environment.ec.europa.eu/topics/industrial-emissions-and-safety/industrial-emissions-directive_en
